For the chromosome 5, 9 and 19 leads, array expansion and ancestry background are candidate explanations; the chromosome 8 association remains significant after adjustment for array length (Extended Data Fig. 1, Supplementary Note 7). Centromeric structural variation on chromosome 8 is therefore associated with the position of the likely kinetochore assembly site.

2.5 Imputed centromeric SVs extend association testing to 630 individuals with expression data

We next extended the analysis beyond centromeric chromatin to gene expression and splicing.

We imputed SVs with CV R² ≥ 0.1 into 630 unrelated 1000 Genomes individuals with matched multi-ancestry gene expression (MAGE) data [Taylor et al., 2024] (Methods). After filtering to common SVs (frequency in [0.05, 0.99]), we tested imputed SV dosage for association with splicing and with gene expression in cis and trans (Methods).

2.6 Centromeric SVs associate with expression or splicing of 141 genes, including 13 distal genes on the same chromosome

We analyzed genes on the same chromosome separately from genes on other chromosomes and distinguished proximal (±10 Mb) from more distal same-chromosome genes.

Centromeric SVs were associated with 86 eGenes and 74 sGenes in cis (each SV's own chro-mosome; Methods) at q < 0.05 (141 unique genes; Figure 5a). Fourteen of these (3 eGenes and 11 sGenes) were undetected by the MAGE consortium's own SNP-based cis-QTL analysis at q < 0.05. Two further definitions of centromeric variation, short-read k-mer haplogroups (ascairn [Shiraishi et al., 2026]; 728 individuals) and α-satellite higher-order repeat variants called in the same assemblies (StV [Altemose et al., 2022]; the same 630 individuals), identified cis-eGene and cis-sGene sets of which two-thirds or more fell within ours (Supplementary Note 5).

We observed that a 2,057-bp insertion within the active chromosome X α-satellite array was associated with expression of SUV39H1 (cis-eQTL q = 1.5 × 10 -2 ; CV R² = 0.17). Notably, SUV39H1 encodes an H3K9 methyltransferase that helps establish and maintain centromeric heterochromatin [Rea et al., 2000 , Peters et al., 2001 , Ma et al., 2024 , Carty et al., 2026 , Sidhwani et al., 2025]. This association indicates a connection between structural variation within an active centromeric array and the expression of a key regulator of centromeric heterochromatin.

Several associations extended far beyond the pericentromeric region. Thirteen genes at 10 loci lay at least 10 Mb from both the centromere and the nearest tag SNP, at distances of 12.2-132.4 Mb, and all of these associations persisted after conditioning on the local tag SNPs (Supplementary Note 6). On chromosome 20, distinct centromeric SVs were associated with splicing of TTPAL, PLTP and NEURL2, 14-16 Mb from the centromere and 13-15 Mb from the nearest tag SNP (cis-sQTL q = 3.1 × 10 -3 , 2.7 × 10 -2 and 3.9 × 10 -2 , respectively; Figure 5c).

In contrast, zero trans associations survived multiple-testing and paralog-mismapping controls (Supplementary Fig. S6; Supplementary Note 6). Thus, the associations detected here were confined to the same chromosome, with some extending far beyond the ±10 Mb region.

In summary, common structural variation in the centromere associates with distal gene expression and splicing on the same chromosomes, and these associations persisted after conditioning on the tag SNPs used to impute the SVs (Supplementary Note 6).

2.7 Imputed centromeric SVs associate with 27 clinical phenotypes in All of Us

Imputation also makes centromeric variation accessible to phenome-wide analysis at biobank scale.

We imputed centromeric SV dosages into All of Us [All of Us Research Program Genomics

Investigators, 2024] using WGS-derived tag SNP genotypes and tested them across both casecontrol and quantitative phenotypes. We scored 10,799 of the 11,129 SV predictors and tested them against 2,417 phecodeX [Shuey et al., 2023] definitions, for a total of 26.1 million SVtrait tests. Sample sizes ranged from 123,760 to 315,204 participants across traits (Methods).

Association statistics were well calibrated across the phenome-wide analysis (λ GC = 1.035), and all 7.5 million tests of a prespecified set of 3,097 negative-control SV predictors had q ≥ 0.10 (Figure 6b; Methods).

We identified 170 SV-clinical phenotype associations (q < 0.05) involving 61 SV predictors and 27 clinical phenotypes, with another 85 associations at q < 0.10 (Figure 6a; Supplementary Note 8). The strongest association connected a chromosome-16 deletion to psychoactive substance-related disorders (OR = 0.79, P = 1.5 × 10 -16 ; 26,943 cases). The same deletion was associated with two additional substance-use clinical phenotypes. Across all significant associations, odds ratios ranged from 0.33 to 2.00, with a median of 0.81.

The associations spanned 12 chromosomes. Chromosome 16 contributed 134 of the 170 significant SV-clinical phenotype associations, representing 31 correlated SV predictors and 11 clinical phenotypes (OR 0.56-1.59). Chromosome X contributed another 10 associations (OR 0.61-2.00), and the remaining 26 were distributed across ten autosomes (OR 0.33-1.44; Figure 6c). Outside the chromosome-16 cluster, signals included seven chromosome-1 SV predictors associated with breast cancer (OR 0.64-1.25; 9,124 cases) and associations with hypertension-related phenotypes (OR = 0.86; 103,924 cases; Figure 6a,c). Thus, the phenome-wide results nominate centromeric SVs and their linked variants across several domains of complex-trait biology.

The 3,097 negative-control SV predictors were well imputed and were selected for a null result in the summary-level joint fine-mapping (Supplementary Note 10; Methods). The smallest P value among their 7.5 million tests, 4.5 × 10 -8 , was consistent with the minimum expected by chance. The control set therefore supports the calibration of the overall analysis.

The chromosome-16 signal was concentrated in the AMR ancestry group. Of the 170 significant associations, 138 reached nominal significance in AMR, compared with 12 in EUR, two in AFR, and none in EAS, SAS, or MID (Extended Data Fig. 2a). This concentration arose although the EUR sample was approximately three times larger for these phenotypes. Chromosome 16 also has the highest mean F ST among imputable centromeric SVs (Supplementary Note 12). The chromosome-16 cluster may therefore reflect an ancestry-specific genetic association or other factors, such as ancestry-correlated differences in recruitment, healthcare use, or diagnostic coding.

Because imputed SVs are correlated with the SNPs used to predict them, disease associations cannot automatically be attributed to the SV itself. We therefore jointly fine-mapped each SV with nearby SNPs. A chromosome-1 deletion associated with disorders of fluid and electrolyte balance (q = 0.008) led its credible set at posterior probability 0.999 under all three fine-mapping methods and both variant-panel constructions. Across the 476 fits, an SV was included in a credible set in 69 and led that set in 34, 26 of them under at least two methods; a SNP had the larger statistic in 451 (median margin 1.90 in |z|; Extended Data Fig. 2b), consistent with most SVs sharing their association with linked SNPs.

Taken together, these results show that imputed centromeric SV dosages are associated with complex traits and diseases in large-scale populations.

3 Discussion

Human centromeres have long been excluded from population-scale genomics because α-satellite arrays are technically challenging to analyze. This has greatly inhibited study of genetic variation in the centromere, which plays an essential role in cell division. Here, we show that centromeric SVs are associated with the methylation of the surrounding satellite array, with the position of the likely kinetochore assembly site, with the expression and splicing of genes along the same chromosome, and with complex traits. The analyses of gene expression and complex traits were enabled by imputation. Because suppressed recombination preserves associations between satellite arrays and flanking SNPs, statistical models trained on the 188 long-read HPRC assemblies with matched SNP genotypes aligned to CHM13 can impute centromeric SV dosage from pericentromeric SNPs in genotyped cohorts with adequate pericentromeric SNP coverage.

Imputation thereby brings these otherwise difficult-to-measure SVs into existing population cohorts with short-read sequencing or genotype arrays, extending previous work imputing short tandem repeats, variable-number tandem repeats, and structural variants from SNP haplotypes [Saini et al., 2018 , Gymrek et al., 2016 , Fotsing et al., 2019 , Bakhtiari et al., 2021 , Mukamel et al., 2021 , Bai et al., 2026 , Noyvert et al., 2025]. Complementary k-mer approaches infer centromere haplogroups or structural features directly from short reads [Shiraishi et al., 2026 , Hain et al., 2026]. Our observations permit four conclusions.

First, centromeric deletions are strongly linked to hypomethylation domains (SHEDs) in proximal satellite sequence. Experimental depletion of DNA methylation alters CENP-A localization and chromosome stability [Salinas-Luypaert et al., 2025]. The methylation associations were concentrated near the tested SV, and among deletion-CpG pairs within 5 Mb, increasing deletion dosage was associated with lower methylation in nearly all cases. We note that three mechanisms would be consistent with this observation: 1. deletions may alter local methylation; 2. the deletion and the hypomethylation may both reflect linked variants or a broader property of the underlying haplotype; 3. methylation state may shape which deletions arise or persist.

Second, centromeric SVs are also associated with the position of the likely kinetochore assembly site. On chromosome 8, a 113-bp deletion and linked variants were associated with the position of the centromere dip region (CDR), the hypomethylated interval that overlaps CENP-A chromatin [Altemose et al., 2022]. The positional association was separable from array length, dip extent, and overall methylation, which suggests that the location of the functional centromere can vary independently of the amount of hypomethylated sequence. Recent populationscale studies using orthogonal approaches observed a similar result, connecting chromosome-8 centromere structure to CDR position [Sun et al., 2026 , Gao et al., 2026]. Although the CDRassociated 113-bp deletion on chromosome 8 was well imputed, we found little evidence that it was associated with complex traits, consistent with common variation in CDR position on chromosome 8 being tolerated at the level of complex traits. However, the CDR is located preferentially toward one end of the active array on some chromosomes, which is compatible with a model of selection favoring biased kinetochore assembly site positioning.

Third, centromeric SVs are associated with gene expression and RNA splicing of genes on the same chromosome. Some involved nearby genes, whereas others involved genes far from the centromere and persisted after conditioning on the local tag SNPs, consistent with structural variants influencing the regulation of multiple genes [Scott et al., 2021]. An informative example linked a chromosome-X centromeric insertion to expression of SUV39H1, which encodes an H3K9 methyltransferase involved in establishing and maintaining pericentromeric heterochromatin [Rea et al., 2000 , Peters et al., 2001]. Its recruitment to pericentromeric DNA and role in maintaining the boundary of CENP-A chromatin connect this association to centromere organization [Ma et al., 2024 , Carty et al., 2026 , Sidhwani et al., 2025]. Combined with the methylation associations, this result raises the possibility that centromeric SVs influence centromeric chromatin both through methylation of the surrounding satellite array and through expression of a gene whose product helps maintain centromeric heterochromatin. More distant associations, including the chromosome-20 splicing signals, suggest candidate mechanisms involving intermediate regulatory genes and long-range chromatin organization.

Fourth, beyond molecular phenotypes, centromeric SVs are associated with complex traits.

In All of Us, associations with clinical phenotypes as diverse as substance-related disorders and breast cancer point to centromeric SVs as candidate contributors to complex-trait variation. These observations led us to ask: how is it that the centromere, which contains no protein-coding genes, might influence complex traits? We suspect that this contribution is driven primarily by proximal mechanisms, in which centromeric variation alters the methylation and heterochromatin landscape in pericentromeric regions, thus altering the regulation of pericentromeric protein coding genes in cis, which may in turn affect downstream genes in trans.

Four limitations of this work define directions for future study. First, high sequence identity within HOR arrays limits both the recall and precision of SV calling in centromeres. In simulations, recall was strong for insertions, deletions and duplications up to 1 kb and declined for larger changes and greater sequence divergence from CHM13. In contrast, large SVs were often represented as several smaller, incorrect calls. Precision varied substantially among chromosomes, indicating considerable heterogeneity in variant calling difficulty across chromosomes. Our SV catalog should therefore be interpreted as candidate SV calls whose sequence-level reliability depends on event type, size and chromosome context. An incorrectly defined SV can nevertheless mark a centromeric haplotype associated with a molecular or clinical phenotype, because errors in SV definition are highly unlikely to confound association testing with phenotypes. Second, monophyletic SVs are imputed far more accurately than non-monophyletic SVs, and the latter will require dedicated approaches to imputation and analysis. Third, experimental approaches will be needed to partition causality between the SVs and the SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with them. Finally, we imputed SVs with a regularized linear model, and classical HMM-based imputation algorithms and reference panels tuned for centromeric SVs may reach higher accuracy. Limitations in imputation are largely a function of panel size and will ease as long-read pangenome resources grow. The variation captured by complete-centromere assemblies is vast [Logsdon et al., 2024 , Gao et al., 2026], and expanding haplotype-resolved cohorts [Liao et al., 2023] will deepen the resolution, extend imputation to the recurrent variants now beyond reach, and eventually power trait mapping.

Overall, we anticipate that our approach, which enables the characterization of SVs in shortread and genotyping-array-based cohorts, will facilitate the standard inclusion of centromeric SVs in future human genetic association studies.

4 Methods

4.1 Assembly alignment and structural-variant calling

We obtained haplotype-resolved assemblies for 196 HPRC Release 2 individuals [Lucas et al., 2026] and aligned each haplotype to the CHM13 v2.0 reference (chromosomes 1-22 and X from Nurk et al. [2022], chromosome Y from Rhie et al. [2023]) with minimap2 [Li, 2018] in assemblyto-reference mode (preset: asm5, output: -cs, chaining bandwidth for repetitive centromeric sequence: 2 kb, -r2k). We called structural variants genome-wide with SVIM-asm v1.0.3 [Heller and Vingron, 2021] in haploid mode (minimum mapping quality ≥ 20, minimum SV length 10 bp, maximum SV size 500,000 bp, and query and reference gap tolerance 200 bp); events exceeding the maximum SV size are reported as breakends. We then retained calls whose breakpoints fell within the active α-satellite HOR arrays defined by CHM13 v2.0 CenSat v2.1 annotations [Altemose et al., 2022], merged the per-haplotype callsets into a multi-sample cohort VCF, and summed the two haplotypes of each individual into diploid genotypes: 0 (homozygous reference), 1 (heterozygous), or 2 (homozygous alternate). We analyzed 23 chromosomes (chr1-22 and X) through an identical pipeline.

Seven chromosomes (chr1, 5, 13, 14, 19, 21, and 22) contain HOR arrays with cross-chromosome α-satellite homology [Alexandrov et al., 2001 , Shepelev et al., 2015] that can confound haplogroup resolution. We used HiFi-based HPRC assemblies (Supplementary Note 2), and we selected SVIM-asm over the assembly SV caller PAV [Ebert et al., 2021] after comparing both inside active HOR arrays of HG002 (Supplementary Note 1).

4.2 Simulation benchmark.

We introduced SVs of known sequence into the active HOR arrays of CHM13 chromosomes and applied the same alignment and SV-calling pipeline; Supplementary Note 13 defines recall, precision and specificity.

4.3 Haplogroup resolution of centromeric SVs

We developed a per-chromosome phylogenetic approach to assign centromeric SVs to haplotype lineages.

Based on the phased, haplotype-resolved assembly calls, we built a binary presence/absence matrix of SVs across the 2N haplotypes of the N individuals. We computed pairwise cosine distances between haplotypes, where x, y are binary SV vectors for two haplotypes, and built a neighbor-joining (NJ) tree from the distance matrix with scikit-bio [Saitou and Nei, 1987].

At each iteration the NJ algorithm joins the pair of nodes (i, j) that minimizes where n is the current number of nodes, proceeding until the tree is fully resolved.

We midpointrooted the tree and used each internal branch to divide the haplotypes into two groups. For every SV with presence/absence vector s ∈ {0, 1} H across the H haplotypes and each branch-partition indicator b ∈ {0, 1} H , we computed the coefficient of determination the squared Pearson correlation between the SV pattern and the bipartition.

We classified an SV as monophyletic if its best-matching branch reached R² ≥ 0.3 and shared at least ten carriers with that branch.

We genotyped the component as the dosage of those shared carriers and imputed it independently. Because an SV may have multiple origins, we masked the matched carriers and repeated the search on the remaining off-branch carriers. We accepted another monophyletic component whenever a branch reached R² ≥ 0.3 with at least five carriers and recorded any remaining unassignable carriers as a residual component. We left SVs unresolved if their first-pass component shared fewer than ten carriers with any branch or if no branch reached R² ≥ 0.3. For each resolved SV, we retained the multi-allelic record before this procedure as its original (pre-resolution) record.

4.4 Pericentromeric SV-SNP linkage disequilibrium

We measured linkage disequilibrium (LD) between centromeric SVs and flanking SNPs. For each chromosome we assembled a combined panel of haplogroup-resolved centromeric SV genotypes and pericentromeric SNP genotypes in the 188 individuals with both, and computed the pairwise Pearson correlation r between every pair of panel variants. The active α-satellite HOR interval follows the CHM13 v2.0 CenSat annotation [Altemose et al., 2022]; we selected SNPs from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage phased VCFs [Byrska-Bishop et al., 2022] within 100 kb outward of each HOR edge and restricted the analysis to biallelic sites with minor allele frequency ≥ 0.05.

4.5 Pericentromeric SNP extraction

We extracted pericentromeric predictor SNPs from the 1000 Genomes Project high-coverage phased VCFs [Byrska-Bishop et al., 2022] for both the training and imputation-target samples.

For training, we used the 188 HPRC individuals that overlap the 1000 Genomes panel and therefore have both directly assembled centromeric SVs (the response) and short-read SNP genotypes (the predictors). We built and integrated eight candidate models spanning three SNP-selection strategies: • Strategy 1 (fixed genomic interval): SNPs within a fixed distance of 100, 200, or 500 kb outward from each centromere boundary.

We defined centromere boundaries using the UCSC hg38 cytoBand [Furey and Haussler, 2003] annotation [Kent et al., 2002], merging each chromosome's p-and q-arm acen bands. We manually adjusted the intervals for chr1, chr2, chr6 and chrX (by 0.7-3.0 Mb; Supplementary Table S13).

• Strategy 2 (boundary-anchored SNP count): the nearest 500, 1,000, or 2,000 SNPs on each side of the centromere boundary, searched up to 20 Mb outward.

• Strategy 3 (midpoint-anchored SNP count): the nearest 500 or 1,000 SNPs on each side of the GRCh38 centromere middle position.

Two ensembles integrated these candidates by retaining, per SV, the single model with the highest cross-validated R² : the best of six candidate models (Strategies 1 and 2, at three settings each, all anchored at the centromere boundary) and the best of eight (adding the two Strategy 3 models, anchored at the midpoint); we used the best-of-eight ensemble in the main analysis.

Heterochromatin-aware flanking. Several centromeres are adjacent to large, SNP-sparse pericentromeric heterochromatin blocks (e.g., 1q12, 7qh, 9q12, 11p). For the fixed-interval strategy (Strategy 1) we therefore adopted chromosome-specific boundaries: we extended a centromere edge outward to include an adjacent heterochromatin block when the gap between the block and the boundary was ≤ 1 Mb, before applying the flanking interval. We used unadjusted boundaries for the remaining chromosomes: 16 of 19 have no heterochromatin block within 1 Mb, and for the other three (chr2, chr16, chr21) we retained the unadjusted boundary.

We retained biallelic SNPs with minor allele frequency ≥ 0.05 and < 5% missing genotypes.

4.6 SV genotype prediction with an elastic-net model

For each SV we trained a separate elastic-net model predicting its genotype from the extracted pericentromeric SNP genotypes. The elastic net [Zou and Hastie, 2005] minimizes where y ∈ {0, 1, 2} n is the SV genotype vector, X is the standardized SNP genotype matrix, α is the regularization strength, and ρ (the l1_ratio) balances the L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) penalties.

We standardized SNP features to zero mean and unit variance (StandardScaler, scikit-learn [Pedregosa et al., 2011]); we used SV genotypes in raw integer form. The unpenalized intercept β 0 used for prediction (Eq. 6) is fit separately by scikit-learn and is omitted from Eq. 4.

We selected hyperparameters by cross-validation (scikit-learn ElasticNetCV, max_iter = 2000) over ρ ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 1.0} and 50 automatically spaced α values per ρ, using K = 4 folds (KFold, shuffled, random_state = 42); we chose the combination minimizing mean crossvalidated squared error (MSE). We filtered SVs to carrier frequency in [0.05, 0.99] before training, and predictor SNPs to carrier frequency ≥ 0.05.

The main quality metric was the cross-validated R² , computed from held-out fold predictions against observed genotypes [Marchini and Howie, 2010, Das et al., 2016].

We trained models on the 188 HPRC individuals with both long-read-assembled centromeric SV genotypes and short-read-genotyped pericentromeric SNPs. We benchmarked the per-SV elastic net against a Beagle v5 reference-panel copying model on an assembly-cophased reference panel, with the identical shared SNP set, effective population size n e = 2000, and leave-one-out affine recalibration of Beagle's posterior dosage (Supplementary Note 4).

4.7 Determinants of SV imputability

For each imputed SV we assembled per-SV features in four groups: intrinsic SV properties (length, carrier frequency, homozygous-alternate count, SV type), locus/cis-region properties (number and distance of available predictor SNPs), chromosome-level properties (active HOR span, number of HOR intervals, pericentromeric flank length, acrocentric status), and locus mapping-quality properties (mean MAPQ, fraction of secondary contig alignments, contig count, and edit distance at the SV locus). We related these to the best-of-eight ensemble cross-validated R² and to the binary imputability thresholds (R² ≥ 0.1 and ≥ 0.3). We fit three complementary models: (i) a univariate association analysis (Spearman rank correlation and, for binary outcomes, ROC-AUC); (ii) a linear mixed-effects model with fixed effects for the numeric features and a per-chromosome random intercept; and (iii) a gradient-boosted regression/classification model (HistGradientBoostingRegressor/Classifier) with feature importances estimated by permutation importance on a held-out test split. We reported model-output diagnostics (e.g., the number of nonzero coefficients) separately and excluded them from the predictor set. We also compared reproducibility of imputable and unimputable SVs in the Q100 HG002 v1.1 assembly (Supplementary Note 3).

4.8 SV dosage imputation into 1000 Genomes samples

We selected imputation target samples from the 1000 Genomes high-coverage cohort by excluding the HPRC training individuals, all members of their families, and non-founder (offspring) individuals, then intersecting with the samples with matched MAGE expression data, leaving 630 unrelated samples (AFR 159, EUR 135, EAS 127, SAS 118, AMR 91). For each chromosome, we extracted SNP genotypes at the exact training positions from the 1000 Genomes phased VCFs [Byrska-Bishop et al., 2022]. Matching required identical chromosome, position, reference, and alternate alleles; we assigned absent or allele-mismatched target SNPs the homozygous-reference genotype (0) before standardization. We scaled target SNP genotypes with the training-fitted

StandardScaler and predicted SV dosages as

We retained SVs with CV R² ≥ 0.1 and further required SV carrier frequency in [0.05, 0.99] among the 630 samples before QTL association testing.

4.9 Cis-and trans-QTL association testing

We obtained expression and splicing phenotypes from MAGE v1.0 [Taylor et al., 2024], lymphoblastoid cell-line RNA-seq of 1000 Genomes individuals (inverse-normal-transformed, TMMnormalized expression for 20,154 genes; LeafCutter [Li et al., 2018b] intron-excision ratios for splicing). Association testing used tensorQTL [Taylor-Weiner et al., 2019]. For each SV-gene pair we fit the linear model where y j is the normalized phenotype, g i the imputed SV dosage, and C the covariates (sex, 5 genotype PCs, and 60 PEER factors [Stegle et al., 2012] for expression or 15 for splicing).

We treated genes on the SV's own chromosome as cis (covering both the conventional ±10 Mb region around the centromere and the remainder of that chromosome) and genes on all other chromosomes as trans. For cis genes, per-gene significance used 10,000 permutations with a Beta-distribution approximation [Ongen et al., 2016], and cross-gene correction used q values To identify genes detected only by the SV analysis, we compared significant SV-associated genes with the MAGE consortium's SNP-based cis-QTL results. We classified genes significant in our analysis and absent from the MAGE set of genes with a significant SNP-based cis-QTL (q < 0.05) as novel.

We also evaluated two alternative genotyping methods with the same QTL mapping (Supplementary Note 5). StV [Altemose et al., 2022] defines variants from α-satellite higher-order repeat monomer organization using HumAS-HMMER HOR monomer annotations. ascairn [Shiraishi et al., 2026] infers centromere haplogroups from short-read k-mer content using their published panel of assembled active-HOR haplotypes. We imputed StV dosages using the same procedure and tested both approaches with the main association-testing framework.

4.10 Methylation-QTL association testing

Methylation and genotype data. Haplotype-resolved whole-genome CpG methylation (5mC bedMethyl) from the 1000 Genomes ONT Sequencing Consortium data release (s3://1000g-ont/PROCESSED_DATA/ALIGNED_TO_HG38/MODKIT/) [Gustafson et al., 2024] provided the phenotype. We retained CpGs with ≥ 10× coverage and a methylation call in at least 90% of analyzed samples. We genotyped the SVIM-asm catalog sites (see Assembly alignment and structural-variant calling) using CHM13-aligned Nanopore long reads with Sniffles2 v2.7.1 [Smolka et al., 2024]. Of the 176 individuals with methylation data, we included 124 with corresponding long-read genotype data. We imputed missing SV genotypes using the cohort mean dosage for the corresponding SV. We selected catalog SVs for read genotyping if they had q < 0.01 in the imputed-dosage association analysis or a SuSiE [Wang et al., 2020] inclusion probability ≥ 0.8. We included genotyped SVs in the association analysis if they had a depth-qualified call rate ≥ 0.8, an observed allele frequency ≥ 0.01, at least three observed carriers, and a minor allele count ≥ 8. This retained 68 SVs on 19 autosomes, including 37 deletions and 31 insertions.

Genome-wide association testing and multiple-testing correction.

We fit each SV-CpG pair by ordinary least squares: where m ic is the methylation fraction of individual i at CpG c, g is ∈ [0, 2] the alternate-allele dosage of SV s, RINT(•) the rank-inverse-normal transform applied across individuals within each CpG, and x i a covariate vector of sex, five genotype principal components and ten methylation principal components.

We tested a pair only when its complete-case minor-allele count was at least 8. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC3).

We tested associations using RINT-transformed methylation values and estimated effect sizes from the same model fitted to untransformed methylation fractions. Accordingly, effect sizes reported in the Results represent the change in methylation fraction per alternate allele.

We tested each retained SV against all retained CpGs genome-wide, comprising 82,365,801 same-chromosome and 1,570,858,672 off-chromosome tests. We applied Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all SV-CpG pairs, using q < 0.01 for significance. We calibrated the global null distribution using 10,000 replicates of a Mammen score-multiplier wild bootstrap to obtain a maximum-statistic reference distribution. We retained all associations with P ≤ 10 -4 for downstream analyses.

Locality and genomic context. We compared distances between associated CpGs and their source SVs with a null distribution generated from 20,000 permutations. Permutations preserved the number of discoveries per SV and sampled CpGs from each SV's tested-CpG distribution.

For source SVs with at least one associated CpG within 5 Mb, we classified effect direction as predominantly negative if more than half of the raw β estimates within this distance were negative. We evaluated effect direction and magnitude separately for deletions and insertions using a two-sided binomial test of the proportion of predominantly negative SVs against 0.5 and the median |β| within 5 Mb, respectively. We annotated target CpGs with CenSat and classified them as satellite-resident or non-satellite, and by CenSat region into the α-satellite array containing the SV (HOR, diverged HOR and monomeric intervals merged within 500 kb), other centromeric sequence, the pericentromeric flanks (intervals labeled p_arm or q_arm) and sequence beyond the centromere (Supplementary Fig. S12e,f). We counted a CpG as dosageresponsive if its absolute effect in the observed data ranked among the top three effects from the real fit and 60 permuted dosage fits. SHEDs are bins of 2,200 CpGs within 5 Mb of an SV whose proportion of dosage-responsive CpGs, relative to the proportion beyond 20 Mb, exceeds the whole-track permutation envelope (Supplementary Fig. S10).

Conditional analysis of nearby SNP variation.

To assess whether methylation-QTL associations were independent of nearby common SNP variation, we performed conditional analyses using two CHM13-referenced SNP panels: CHM13-aligned long-read variant calls from the 1000 Genomes ONT Sequencing Consortium data release [Gustafson et al., 2024] and the T2T-CHM13 1000 Genomes joint callset. In each panel, we fine-mapped SNPs within 1, 5, 10, and 20 Mb of the source SV using SuSiE [Wang et al., 2020], then tested the SV association conditionally in a cross-fitted analysis with fine-mapping and evaluation in disjoint sample folds. We considered associations robust to local SNP variation if SuSiE supported the SV and a direction-concordant conditional association remained for at least two distances in both panels. Separately, we conditioned associations on the SV's elastic-net imputation score and its non-zero SNP predictors.

Robustness. We applied three sensitivity refits to the discovery set: adjustment for persample CpG read depth, leave-one-carrier-out analysis, and restriction to individuals with observed depth-qualified SV genotypes. The leave-one-carrier-out analysis required each association to retain its sign and at least half of its original |β| in every refit, while the genotype-complete analysis excluded all mean-imputed dosages. We report retention, sign agreement and significance for all three in Supplementary Fig. S14a-c. Genotype composition and Hardy-Weinberg fit for every discovery variant are given in Supplementary Table S12.

Measurement availability. To assess carrier-dependent CpG measurement in the assemblybased HPRC cohort, we matched each discovery CpG to twenty controls on source variant, order of distance, CenSat class, mean methylation and number of valid observations. We then regressed measurement presence on carrier dosage in both sets under a shared correction (Supplementary Fig. S11, Supplementary Note 9). We estimated effect sizes in the discovery cohort alone (Supplementary Note 9).

4.11 Centromere dip region calling and dip-position QTL mapping

CDR calling and annotation. We obtained haplotype-resolved 5mC from modkit bed-Methyl pileups for 384 HPRC Release 2 haplotypes. We restricted modification calls to 5mC alone (Supplementary Note 7). We then computed mean methylation in 5-kb bins in absolute reference coordinates, using bedtools intersect -f 1 [Quinlan and Hall, 2010] to retain bins within the active α-satellite HOR array, defined per sample as the union of the active-HOR intervals of the global centromere annotation [Gao et al., 2026]. We called dips with CDR-Finder [Mastrorosa et al., 2024] at its recommended parameters (thresholds 0.34/0.30, merge distance 1 bp, edge distance 500 kb, baseline 0.4). We merged dips within 150 kb into annotated CDRs as in Gao et al. [2026]. We placed per-haplotype methylation in reference coordinates by walking the SVIM-asm CIGAR strings.

Definition of CDR phenotypes. Writing the active array as [start, end] with covered length L (the summed length of the merged annotated rows) and covered midpoint m, each dip's relative position is (dip covered offset -m)/(L/2), running from -1 at the array start through 0 at its center to +1 at its end. We computed ten phenotypes per (sample, assembly haplotype, chromosome) over the active array only, then averaged them over an individual's two haplotypes and rank-inverse-normal transformed them. They span four axes: position, scatter, abundance and level (Extended Data Table 2). Six of the ten are normalized by array length.

SV association testing. We tested all 11,129 cataloged loci across 23 chromosomes using SV genotypes derived directly from the assemblies. We derived genotypes per chromosome through deterministic haplogroup resolution on a bcftools merge [Danecek et al., 2021] cohort VCF, with cosine-neighbor-joining restricted to the 188 individuals overlapping the methylation cohort before tree construction. We grouped loci with identical genotypes in all 188 samples into 7,276 genotype groups, each with one test statistic, and report results per genotype group.

We tested each SV against each phenotype with 10 ancestry principal components and a basecaller indicator as covariates, under a Freedman-Lane [Freedman and Lane, 1983] permutation null restricted to the same chromosome. Sample size varies by chromosome with methylation overlap (e.g. n = 151 for chromosome 8). The genome-wide test used 10 5 permutations; we re-ran each chromosome-by-phenotype pair with a locus at that floor at 10 7 permutations, and a second round increased the permutations for every remaining pair with a locus within ∼100-fold of the loosest threshold.

We excluded the two sensitivity phenotypes (Extended Data Table 2) from the Bonferroni correction, leaving eight main phenotypes and α = 0.05/(11,129 × 8) = 5.62 × 10 -7.

Array-length and ancestry sensitivity analyses.

Array stability. We tested each lead for associations of dosage with both array endpoints and array length, and excluded leads with dosage-dependent array length for every length-normalized phenotype. We also added the endpoints as covariates. Ancestry. A within-superpopulation random-effects meta-analysis required minor allele frequency ≥ 0.05, at least twelve carriers, at least three informative superpopulations, consistent sign and leave-one-population-out stability. Chromosome X is reported separately and any chromosome-X candidate is sex-adjusted.

We also tested whether total SV burden was associated with CDR phenotypes. We rank- For the chromosome-8 interval we calibrated the statistic directly. Taking the top lead as the conditioning variant, we computed the smallest conditional P over a declared candidate set, then repeated that computation on 2,000 phenotype permutations. The candidate set was the pre-specified leads, meaning the variants that independently reached study-wide significance in the main analysis before any conditioning; an open search over all distinct genotype vectors in chr8:44.2-44.5 Mb is a sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Note 7).

Sequence characterization of the chromosome-8 locus. We decomposed the chromosome-8 active α-satellite array of CHM13 v2.0 into monomers with HORmon v1.0.0 [Kunyavskaya et al., 2022], which identified nine monomer classes, grouped into seven major classes (M1 to M7), and a per-monomer partition of the array. As a sensitivity check we repeated the decomposition with StringDecomposer v1.1.2 [Dvorkina et al., 2020] against the same monomer set. We classified monomers shorter than 150 bp as shortened. We constructed repeat units by cutting the monomer class string at each occurrence of the unit's boundary class. To compare the chromosome-8 count with other centromeres, we applied the same decomposition and the same threshold to all 26 active arrays of the reference, then tested the class distribution of the pooled shortened monomers against class abundance by permutation, with 200,000 draws. We tested class assignment of a shortened monomer against a prefix null of the 927 non-M5 monomers among 1,000 drawn from the same array (Supplementary Note 7).

For each of the 392 HPRC Release 2 haplotype assemblies we mapped two reference coordinates flanking each copy into assembly coordinates by the same SVIM-asm CIGAR walk used for coordinate lifting, then counted assembly bases between them. We assigned spans within 5 bp of a predicted length to that length and treated the remainder as unresolved.

4.12 Biobank-scale association test and fine-mapping in All of Us

Scoring. We applied elastic-net weights to short-read whole-genome genotypes in the All of Us

Research Program [All of Us Research Program Genomics Investigators, 2024] (Controlled Tier, curated data release v8) with plink2 -score [Chang et al., 2015] (variance-standardize), giving a per-participant dosage ĝ = X β. Of 11,129 predictors, we scored 10,799 that were scoreable in the All of Us variant panel. We retained only weight SNPs present in that panel above the MAF threshold and quantified per-SV predictor coverage before any association testing. Imputation accuracy is the cross-validated R² of the model that generated the dosage, estimated in the training cohort by four-fold cross-validation (see SV genotype prediction with an elastic-net model).

Predictor sets. We assigned the 10,799 scored predictors to four pre-specified sets that defined the multiple-testing families: discovery predictors (3,416); negative controls (3,097); newly scoreable predictors with no discovery prior (4,207); and chromosome-X predictors (79).

Negative-control predictors had posterior inclusion probabilities below 0.01 for all 464 traits in the summary-level fine-mapping (Supplementary Note 10) and otherwise follow the identical procedure.

Phenotypes and testing. We defined disease phenotypes using phecodeX. The main definition requires a minimum code count of two (MCC = 2), giving 2,530 phenotypes, of which 2,417 met the testing threshold of at least 50 cases and at least 50 controls. We analyzed the permissive single-code definition (MCC = 1) with the same pipeline as a case-definition sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig. S2). Reported case counts include only participants in the regression, after cohort intersection and sex restriction.

For phenotype j with case indicator y j ∈ {0, 1} n , the covariate matrix is C = [ 1, age splines(3), sex, gPC 1...16 , ancestry dummies(5) ], and the null was fit once per phenotype by iteratively reweighted least squares, giving fitted probabilities μij and weights

Each SV dosage g s was residualized on the covariate basis once per phenotype by the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell identity, so that a single null fit serves every SV.

The Rao score test for H 0 : with βsj = U sj /V sj .

This gave 26,101,183 valid SV-phecode tests. Genomic inflation was computed as λ GC = median(T sj ) χ 2 1, 0.5 with χ 2 1,0.5 = 0.4549. We re-fit every SV-trait pair reaching q < 0.05 or P < 10 -4 under the score test using exact Firth logistic regression [Firth, 1993, Heinze and Schemper, 2002], which maximizes the penalized log-likelihood where I is the Fisher information.

Significance came from the penalized likelihood-ratio test.

When the exact fit did not converge, we substituted an approximate Firth recalibration; all associations reported as significant rest on the exact fit. We then applied Benjamini-Hochberg FDR [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995] within each predictor set: for the m t tests of set t with ordered P (1) ≤ • • • ≤ P (mt) , we declared associations significant up to k = max{ i : P (i) ≤ iα/m t } at α = 0.05. We corrected the negative-control set across its own 7,485,449 tests.

Score-test calibration. We validated the score test against the exact Firth fit within every carrier-count bin and every predictor set.

Per-ancestry analysis. We re-tested every SV-trait pair independently within each of the six ancestry groups, with exact per-ancestry Firth regression and within-group Benjamini-Hochberg correction. To test whether a signal restricted to one ancestry group reflects residual structure inside that group, we recomputed principal components within the AMR group, added them to the null model, and re-fit the association. We also re-fit SV-trait pairs after restricting to unrelated participants.

Quantitative traits. We tested the same predictors against a panel of quantitative laboratory and anthropometric traits, giving 755,930 SV-trait pairs. Each SV-trait pair received a crossancestry classification based on independent per-ancestry fits and an inverse-variance-weighted meta-analysis: consistent (including heterogeneous and power-limited subclasses) where perancestry estimates agree in direction and magnitude, possibly stratified where they do not, discordant where they oppose, and underpowered otherwise.

Chromosome X. The scoring pipeline applies a uniform 0/1/2 map, which for these data is the X-inactivation model. We re-scored chromosome-X SV-trait pairs under three ploidy models (the map in use, halved male dosage, and per-sex standardization) and computed the correlation between dosage and sex under each model.

Fine-mapping. We restricted fine-mapping to unrelated participants (n = 291,668, after removing 23,536 related or otherwise flagged participants, 7.5%), to keep relatedness from inflating the in-sample LD matrix; the EUR (n = 168,174) and AMR (n = 54,387) ancestry groups are nested within it.

We fit each candidate association under two panel constructions. The single-SV construction contains the target SV plus its most strongly correlated tag SNPs (median ∼120); the joint construction additionally includes every same-chromosome SV, so an SV competes against other SVs as well as against SNPs. An SV included in a joint panel is termed a candidate if the disease screen nominated it and a competitor otherwise. We computed identifiability diagnostics on the full panel and after excluding the SV's own elastic-net predictors. We fit each panel with three methods: an individual-level linear-probability model and summary-level fits on linearprobability and on logistic statistics. For each fit, we computed the LD matrix in sample as the correlation of the covariate-residualized dosage matrix. In total, we completed 476 fits.

Credible sets and significance labels. We extracted credible sets uniformly across methods with susie_get_cs at coverage 0.95 and purity threshold min_abs_corr = 0.5, with at most ten components. We labeled fits without a set meeting coverage and purity unresolved.

For each SV, we report credible-set inclusion and the highest posterior within that set separately. The main quantitative discriminator is the margin in |z| between the best SV and the best SNP in the same fit, together with the multiple R² of the SV on its own panel. Negative-control predictors entered fine-mapping panels on the same terms as other SVs.

Methods; Supplementary Note 7. main analysis. Using covariates matched to the main analysis, we tested haplogroup dosages for associations with expression and splicing, including chromosome X, and identified 66 cis-eGenes and 49 cis-sGenes, 46 and 35 of them within the main-analysis 86 and 74 (Table S8; Supplementary Fig. S4a; λ = 1.016 for expression and 1.062 for splicing; 101 unique cis genes).

Of these 101, 73 lie among the 141 cis genes of the main analysis, and 64 genes are common to the main, ascairn and StV routes, whose union spans 200 genes.

Concordance under an α-satellite HOR variant definition. StV [Altemose et al., 2022] called 17,786,321 higher-order repeat instances of 22,652 types across the 384 phased haplotype assemblies, 2,992 of them common. Tested in a QTL analysis that shared the assemblies, the SNP panel, the elastic-net imputation, the 630 individuals and the tensorQTL configuration of the main analysis (Methods), these dosages identified 78 cis-eGenes and 63 cis-sGenes, of which 54 of the 78 and 42 of the 63 fall within the main-analysis 86 and 74 (Supplementary Fig. S4b).

190 of 238 (79.8%) and 179 of 188 (95.2%). All 14 genes distal under both definitions survive on informative fits (R² 0.000-0.142). Conditioning leaves the three chromosome-20 associations intact, shifting them from P = 4.16 × 10 -9 to 3.58 × 10 -9 (TTPAL), 5.42 × 10 -7 to 9.78 × 10 -7 (PLTP ) and 5.96 × 10 -6 to 6.07 × 10 -6 (NEURL2 ).

The paralog control. GRCh38 cross-mappability covers only paralogs present in GRCh38, so a complete-assembly search, also applied to the trans candidate DUSP22 below, was run on the 14 genes distal under both distance metrics, asking whether each has a high-identity copy in the pericentromere of its own chromosome; every query recovered its own locus at identity ≥ 0.98.

Thirteen have no such copy. The exception is WHAMMP1 on chromosome 15, a transcribed processed pseudogene and the most significant of the 14 (q = 7.8×10 -4 ). It has six high-identity copies on chromosome 15 (99.49% at 28.26 Mb, 96.0-96.4% at 20.33, 20.37, 26.51 and 26.55 Mb, 93.4% at 80.67 Mb), two within 3 Mb of the α-satellite array and all at mapping quality 0. We therefore exclude it, leaving 13 distal genes at 10 loci. None of the three chromosome-20 genes has an additional copy anywhere on chromosome 20.

We computed genomic-control λ from the per-gene Beta-approximated permutation P value, pooled across the 23 chromosomes. For expression it is 1.04 in the whole-chromosome region and 1.12 in the ±10 Mb region; for splicing, 1.11 and 1.17 (Supplementary Fig. S8), with Storey π 0 [Storey and Tibshirani, 2003] of 0.98, 0.95, 0.95 and 0.93 respectively.

Trans associations. Across 1.26 × 10 9 SV-phenotype pairs tested in trans, the four controls (multiple testing, cross-mappability, conditioning and the paralog check) remove all 46 target genes.

Over the union of the two imputation ensembles (8 eQTL and 38 sQTL target genes, 46 in total), Benjamini-Hochberg at q < 0.1 applied across all trans tests retains 12 trans target genes and Bonferroni retains 2, whereas a fixed P < 5 × 10 -8 threshold expects ∼63 false positives across these tests, with an empirical false-discovery rate of 59.6% under permutation calibration.

Both Bonferroni-significant genes have paralogs.

In the GRCh38, GENCODE v26 crossmappability tables [Saha and Battle, 2018a,b], HSD17B7 and its pseudogene HSD17B7P2 show a symmetric cross-mappability of 999.5 k-mers. HSD17B7P2 lies inside the chromosome-10 pericentromere, and in our analysis of that table the cross-mapping is 30.8-fold stronger than with the pericentromere of any other chromosome. DUSP22 has a 63.9 kb copy, DUSP22B, that is 99.86% identical, lies 0.82 Mb from the chromosome-16 α-satellite array in CHM13, and is absent from GRCh38, which instead maps that sequence onto chr6:287,496-356,341 at mapping quality 60. Short reads from the unreferenced copy are assigned to chromosome-6 DUSP22, so chromosome-16 pericentromeric SVs linked to that copy appear as trans regulators.

The lncRNA overlapping the DUSP22 promoter (ENSG00000287265) has a 99.78%-identical copy at the same chromosome-16 locus and shows the same association, whereas EXOC2, a chromosome-6p25.3 neighbor 0.2 Mb away with no chromosome-16 paralog, has no chromosome-16 SNP below P = 1 × 10 -5 . The same mismapping mechanism accounts for an estimated 6.1% of trans-eQTLs in this cohort [Aqil et al., 2026].

Of the 46 target genes, 12 remain after Benjamini-Hochberg, 2 after Bonferroni, 1 after cross-mappability, which removes HSD17B7, 1 after conditioning, and 0 after the non-referenceparalog check, which removes DUSP22. No trans association survives all four controls. POU2F1 fails Benjamini-Hochberg, fails Bonferroni, and survives conditioning in 0 of 6 pairs; MCOLN2 fails both thresholds and cross-maps at 20.5 with PXMP4.

Sequence at the chromosome-8 locus

Class assignment of the partial monomer. We assigned the 112 bp monomer to a class by globally aligning its first 112 bases to the first 112 bases of each class consensus, with identity taken as matches over alignment length. Its identity to the M5 consensus exceeded that of all 927 other-class monomers among 1,000 drawn from the same array (P = 0.001); in two additional null comparisons a 112 bp prefix reaches a median identity of 0.97 to its best class and the observed identity difference from the second-best class lies below the null median. The prefix-based assignment identifies a monomer's own class in 94.2% of the 1,000 draws and in every M5 draw. Dvorkina et al. [2021] previously reported a partial monomer of this length in this array.

The monomer across haplotype assemblies. We measured the span between fixed anchors at each of the three copies in 392 HPRC Release 2 haplotype assemblies (Methods). At the first two copies the two states differ by 113 bp, which spans the 112 bp monomer and one adjacent base, and CHM13 has the longer state at both (482 against 369 bp, 128 and 221 haplotypes; 596 against 483 bp, 91 and 257). At the third copy the states differ by 58 bp and CHM13 has the shorter one (311 against 369 bp, 78 and 272). The 199 bp span expected if the monomer were absent at the third copy was not observed in any of the 350 resolved haplotypes. We resolved the three spans in 349, 348 and 350 of 392 haplotypes, respectively. Aligning each extracted span to the reference span places the 58 bp within the shortened monomer in all 274 haplotypes with the longer state, at monomer position 109 in 267 of them and 107 in the remaining 7, and none of the flanking M2 or M3.1 monomers contains it; the shortened monomer occupies 112 of the 311 bases of the measured span. The 58 bp matches M5 monomers of this array from position 109, and M5 accounts for the 100 highest-scoring placements. Since 112 and 58 sum to 170, the modal M5 length of this array, the two states at the third copy correspond to a shortened and a full-length monomer. Probes of the same length drawn from full-length M5 monomers at known positions each recovered the position they were drawn from, which establishes that the placement resolves position within a monomer (Supplementary Fig. S16). At the 113-bp deletion itself, assembly sequence agreed with the SVIM-asm genotype in 330 of the 337 haplotypes with an unambiguous allele assignment (97.9%).

Shortened monomers across the reference.

To compare the chromosome-8 count with other centromeres we applied the same decomposition and the same length threshold to all 26 active arrays of the reference, giving 255,245 monomers, and tested the class distribution of the pooled short monomers against class abundance by permutation with 200,000 draws. The class distribution differs from that expected from monomer abundance (P = 5 × 10 -6 ), with class M5 at 7.2 times its expected count and M4 at 7.6.

Operational definitions.

We classified monomers shorter than 150 bp as truncated. On the chromosome-8 array the four such monomers, including the three partial-monomer copies, fall between 112 and 124 bp and the next shortest measures 161 bp. We identified CENP-B boxes as matches to NTTCGNNNNANNCGGGN on either strand. Four of the array's 5,263 boxes have adenine at the first position of the motif, and two of the three truncated copies contain one each.

Dip measurement

Dip calling and dip counts. Calling the CDR within each sample's active HOR array [Gao et al., 2026] gives ∼22,000 dips, 57 per haplotype across a median of 13 assembled centromeres and ∼4 per centromere, and merging dips within 150 kb gives a mean of 1.07 annotated CDRs per active array (93.1% with exactly one). A concurrent survey reported one kinetochore site in 94% of centromeres genome-wide and in 98% of chromosome-8 haplotypes, each spanning a mean of 4.3 methylation dips [Gao et al., 2026]. The position association is retained with a single main dip per haplotype (P = 7.5 × 10 -4 ) and with the deepest dip (t = -6.19). Over the whole centromeric satellite block the same caller and parameters produce ∼324,000 dips (median 880 per haplotype, ∼50 per centromere), against a literature expectation of one to three; at thresholds 0.5/0.5 the R10.4.1 subset gives 2.2-2.5 dips per centromere.

Chromosome-specific dip position.

Where the dip falls along the array differs by chromosome: 19 of the 23 chromosomes place it preferentially on one side, and all five acrocentrics place it on the p side (Supplementary Table S9). On chromosomes 6, 10, 12, 19 and X the dips resolve into two preferred positions, recovered in independent halves of the cohort. The lower falls between 0.07 and 0.19 on all five and the upper between 0.74 and 0.94 on chromosomes 6, 10, 12 and 19, placing both within a few hundred kilobases of an array end (Supplementary Table S10).

pericentromeric dosages, while the discovery predictors give 99 significant associations from a comparable 8,256,472 tests.

The 3,097 negative-control predictors occupy 11 chromosomes, including 1,884 on chromosome 19 and none on chromosomes 16 or X. We selected them for a null result in the summarylevel association analysis (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Twenty-eight SV-phecode pairs from the range0.05 ≤ q < 0.10 are significant in more than one ancestry group, over 27 SVs at 14 loci, and all 28 survive restriction to unrelated participants.

Strong quantitative-trait associations are consistent across ancestry groups. Of 755,930 SV-trait pairs, 56,169 are consistent across ancestry groups and 589,607 underpowered. Among SV-trait pairs reaching meta P < 10 -4 , consistency runs from 102 of 104 systolic blood-pressure pairs (98.1%) and 253 of 273 heart-rate pairs (92.7%) to 70 of 83 diastolic pairs (84.3%) and 67 of 89 hip-circumference pairs (75.3%) (Extended Data Fig. 2c). On the same anthropometric trait the negative-control predictors are consistent in 166 of 300 SV-trait pairs (55.3%), against 239 of 308 (77.6%) for discovery predictors, and the comparison gives OR = 2.80 (P = 6.7 × 10 -9 ). Strong quantitative-trait associations are therefore more consistent across ancestry groups than those of the negative-control predictors.

All 11 chromosome-X associations at q < 0.10 remain significant under each of the three ploidy models.

Fine-mapping. We fine-mapped every candidate association against its own tag SNPs in the unrelated subset (n = 291,668), producing 476 fits under two panel constructions and three methods (Methods). The imputed SVs are strongly correlated with their local SNPs: the multiple R² of an SV on its own SNP panel has median 0.900, and 0.807 when the SNPs that built the dosage are excluded.

Credible-set composition. Among the single-SV credible sets that contain an SV, 12 contain the SV alone and 42 contain it together with a SNP outside its imputation predictors, while 7 contain it with only its own imputation predictors, which cannot distinguish the SV dosage from the SNPs used to predict it. We included five negative-control predictors in four fits, and two of those fits placed a control SV in a credible set, showing that credible-set assignment can arise without signal. S10.4 Structural-variant analysis set and elastic-net imputation

SV calling. We called structural variants from the n = 196 assembly-based cohort (1000 Genomes NYGC and HPRC assemblies) with SVIM-asm and harmonized the calls into a haplogroup-resolution catalog (main Methods). Resolution assigns each event one of four categories, named as in the released tables (non_decomposed, monophyletic, original_decomposed, residual); by design no de-duplication is performed across categories, so a genomic event may be included in the pipeline as more than one test row.

Per-SV elastic-net predictors. For each SV we trained an elastic-net regression of SV dosage on local SNP genotypes. Let x ∈ R p be the (standardized) genotypes of p pericentromeric SNPs and y the SV dosage. We fit with the penalty mixing ρ ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 1.0} and strength α chosen by 4-fold cross-validation (ElasticNetCV, 50 candidate α, seed 42).

We trained eight candidate models per SV (Section 4.5) and selected the model with the highest cross-validated R² (CV R² ) as the main predictor (best-of-eight). Two of the eight use SNPs anchored at the array midpoint, and an SV whose best-performing model was one of those two additionally has a sensitivity predictor built from the best of the remaining six (best-of-six); an SV whose two selections are identical contributes a single predictor. The unit of analysis is therefore the predictor, nested within the SV, and 11,129 candidate predictors are evaluated by the admissibility filter.

The coefficients βstd are in standardized-genotype units and are used directly as the predictor weights β = βstd throughout the cTWAS model (Section S10.6), paired with the reference correlation matrix R. This is the FUSION/cTWAS convention [Gusev et al., 2016 , Zhao et al., 2024]: with both the predictor and R on standardized genotypes, the imputed-feature z-score z SV = β ⊤ z/ β ⊤ R β requires no per-SNP standard-deviation factor, which the full S-PrediXcan identity [Barbeira et al., 2018] includes for per-dosage PredictDB-style weights. The two pa-rameterizations are ≈ 0.98 correlated under the null but can differ by up to ∼ 2× on individual realized statistics. CV R² measures how well an SV is tagged by SNPs and therefore (Section S10.11) how distinguishable the SV is from those SNPs in fine-mapping.

Inclusion filter. The 11,129 candidate predictors all have CV R² ≥ 0.1 from model selection.

We applied three additional filters: autosomal only (chromosome X lacks a b38 LD reference; 79 excluded, leaving 11,050); at least one weight SNP matching the b38 LD-reference variant info on (chrom, pos, ref, alt) (4,075 excluded, leaving 6,975); and at least three matched weight SNPs within a single LDetect-b38 block (456 excluded). The filter includes 6,519 predictors on 5,149 distinct SVs (4,195 best-of-eight, 2,324 best-of-six; 2,825 SVs by best-of-eight alone, 954 by best-of-six alone, 1,370 by both), the analysis set (Table S16).

Included predictors occupy 23 pericentromeric super-regions distributed over 21 chromosomes: chromosomes 6 and 11 each contribute two disjoint super-regions, and two chromosomes contribute none. Chromosome X is excluded by construction, and all 239 chromosome-14 candidates fail the LD-reference matching test. Their weight SNPs have a median of zero matched variants (maximum one), so no chromosome-14 predictor can be placed on the reference panel. This exclusion reflects reference-panel matching rather than low imputation accuracy: chromosome-14 candidate CV R² has a median of 0.23 and reaches 0.95.

S10.7 Rank deficiency and numerical safeguards

Writing p+G) , the construction in Eq. ( 14) is exactly a congruence transform i.e.

R aug is rank-deficient by construction: each SV row is a deterministic linear combination of the SNP rows. This is the cTWAS augmentation identity, and it has two consequences. (i) Diagnostics computed within the augmented space (e.g. an estimate_s_rss z-R consistency check on the SV row) are not independent, because the SV row is by definition consistent with the SNP rows from which it was formed; such checks are implementation checks, not independent evidence. (ii) The imputed SV adds zero independent degrees of freedom: deterministic function of the SNP z-scores, with no independently measured component.

An imputed SV is therefore non-identifiable at the SV level: it can never be distinguished from the SNP linear combination it equals. It differs from a measured SNP, whose z-score, though correlated with its LD neighbours, has independent sampling variation given them (Var(z j | z -j ) > 0). Fine-mapping may still assign such an SV a high PIP when it is the most compact summary of a diffuse signal, but a high PIP then reflects summarization, not SV-specific causation. The question is thus one of identifiability, quantified in Sections S10.11-S10.13.

SuSiE-RSS operates directly on the unregularized rank-deficient canonical correlation matrix, whose smallest eigenvalue lies at numerical zero because the augmentation is rank-deficient by at least G (Eq. 18).

S10.8 SuSiE-RSS fine-mapping procedure

Joint fine-mapping used SuSiE-RSS [Wang et al., 2020 , Zou et al., 2022], the sum-of-single-effects regression-with-summary-statistics model. The augmented effect vector is the sum of L single effects, each γ ℓ a one-hot "which variable" indicator with posterior inclusion probabilities (the variational single-effect posterior) α ℓj = Pr(γ ℓj = 1 | data).

S10.9 GWAS harmonization and missing-support handling

For each (super-region, GWAS) pair, we retrieved GWAS rows in the region with tabix and harmonized them to the panel: variant identifiers chr_pos_ref_alt were parsed to canonical chrom:pos:ref:alt, matched to panel SNP identifiers, and z-scores sign-flipped on REF/ALT swaps. In these regions many panel SNPs with a predictor weight are absent from the GWAS (for some SVs a median of ∼ 84% of the support is missing). We compared three approaches to missing summary statistics (Table S18) and treated their discordance as a diagnostic.

Summary-statistic imputation (IMPUTE).

We imputed missing SNP z-scores with the ImpG Gaussian-process estimator [Pasaniuc et al., 2014], implemented in its maintained successor ssimp 0.5.5 [Rüeger et al., 2018]: ẑu = Σ ut (Σ tt + λI) -1 z t for untyped variant u given typed

S10.11 Power and limits of SV identifiability

To bound sensitivity we simulated each SV's EN predictor as the causal genotype and measured power. The simulated causal unit is exactly the predicted dosage β ⊤ g, so a real SV, which deviates from its predictor by imputation error, is harder to distinguish from SNP effects: this is an upper bound on identifiability for the augmented model. Simulating the predictor as causal induces SNP z-scores z i = (Rβ) i λ/D with E[z SV ] = λ; we swept the signal strength λ ∈ {4, 6, 8} (230 draws each) and recorded power(τ ) = Pr(causal-unit PIP ≥ τ ) (Table S20; Supplementary Fig. S20b,c).

Power is low even at z ≈ 8 (≤ 35%), and power decreases with imputability: SVs with CV R² ≥ 0.6 reach the PIP threshold in only 5-10%, versus 31-40% for CV R² < 0.4. This is an identifiability ceiling, not a weak-signal artifact: a well-imputed SV is well-tagged by SNPs, so fine-mapping distributes the posterior probability across the SV and its correlated tag SNPs, leaving no single variant with high PIP.

Increasing sample size raises λ ∝ √ N but does not remove the CV R² ceiling for well-imputed SVs. Two corollaries follow: (i) a high-PIP imputed SV is preferentially a poorly imputed one (low CV R² ), and so the SV least trustworthy as a genotype proxy; (ii) testing more traits does not by itself resolve this ambiguity, even in larger cohorts.

S10.12 Phenome-wide application

For each fit we stored every variable with PIP ≥ 0.01, a per-(region, trait, handling) summary, and an automated selection across the two approaches (Table S21). We selected a row as a candidate only if it met thresholds under both approaches (IMPUTE PIP ≥ 0.5 and MATCHED PIP ≥ 0.5), the fit converged, and at most three SVs in the region×trait reached PIP ≥ 0.5.

Several correlated SV rows can reach high posterior in one super-region because each decomposition category is included separately (Section S10.4), so one genomic event may appear in a fit more than once. More SV-trait pairs reach the PIP threshold under MATCHED than under IMPUTE (Table S21), because restricting the predictor to SNPs with available summary statistics changes the predicted dosage. A MATCHED predictor therefore represents only the component of SV dosage predicted by the observed SNPs. The two approaches share weights B and LD R, so their agreement measures robustness to the treatment of missing summary statistics.

S10.13 Identifiability audit: own-tag conditioning and ancestry-matched LD

We assessed each candidate SV to determine whether its signal is specific to the SV or reflects tagging SNPs.

Own-tag conditioning. For SV g we ranked SNPs by their augmented correlation with the , and took the top-K (K ≤ 40) as the SV's own tags S. Using the multivariate-normal conditional under R aug , the SV z-score conditioned on its own tags is

A signal with low retention is a proxy for its own tag SNPs (SNP-non-identifiable). High retention is consistent with an SV-specific signal but does not establish one, so the screen is one-sided.

Two controls calibrate it. As a positive control, a known proxy deletion on chromosome 3 falls to 7% retention at the full tag set (K = 40). As a negative control for specificity, simulating a single causal tag SNP (a true single-SNP proxy) reduces retention to 0.000 at every K, whereas simulating the SV's own predictor as the causal unit retains 0.3-0.8 (mean 0.62 at K=10). The known proxy shows marked attenuation after conditioning, whereas unresolved candidates retain more of their association, so the audit separates the two. The distinction is less clear at low CV R² (a simulated causal low-CV-R² SV can retain as little as 0.32), and at very low panel size the R aug [S, S] -1 inverse is numerically unstable.

Ancestry-matched LD. For the candidates surviving own-tag conditioning, we rebuilt R from 1000 Genomes subsets matched to the GWAS ancestry (FIN n = 99; EUR n = 503), holding β and z fixed so that only the denominator D g in Eq. 13 changes. An internal control (1000 Genomes EUR ≈ the EUR-525 reference panel) agreed, z SV moved by at most 18% across the surviving candidates, and at n = 99 the own-tag inverse was numerically unstable (retention > 2000%); FinnGen in-sample LD or direct WGS or long-read SV genotyping is the decisive test of SV-specificity.

Of the 24 candidates, 21 were SNP-non-identifiable (12 whose associations attenuated after conditioning on their tag SNPs, 7 explained by a stronger regional SNP, and 2 SNP-equivalent at CV R² ≥ 0.6), and three remained unresolved (chr12 sv721 with standing height, CV R² = 0.15, z SV = 7.04 against a strongest regional SNP of 5.77; chr11 sv263 with BMI, 0.43, -6.26 against 4.86; chr11 sv271 with serum albumin, 0.41, -6.02 against 4.33), each with |z SV | above any single regional SNP, retained under own-tag conditioning and stable under ancestry-matched LD.

The result is therefore identifiability-limited (21 SNP-non-identifiable and 3 WGS-unresolved candidates), and determining whether the signal is specific to an SV at these pericentromeric loci requires WGS or long-read SV genotyping. and the SV-SV block β ⊤ Rβ/(D i D j ), with D j = β ⊤ j Rβ j the induced SV standard deviation, so the SV-SV diagonal is 1 by construction. Because every SV row is a linear combination of SNP rows, R aug is rank-deficient by construction, the algebraic origin of the non-identifiability quantified in this note. S19-S20.

Dense-panel identifiability validation.

Measurement presence in the interval-based test. The interval-based test of local methylation includes a coverage negative control, but we compute that control only among samples that produced a value, so the control conditions on measurement presence. We repeated the test's design with measurement presence as the outcome, on the same 11,129 loci and 150 individuals under the same covariates and Freedman-Lane permutation null. SV dosage predicts whether an interval has a methylation value at 14.7%, 12.6% and 12.3% of loci at ±10, ±50 and ±100 kb, against a 5% nominal rate and against 8.2%, 8.4% and 8.2% for the depth control on the same loci (genomic control factors 1.84, 1.60 and 1.54). The direction depends on interval width: among significant loci, 27.4% have a negative slope at ±10 kb against 57.8% at ±100 kb. Both insertions and deletions show associations in either direction: at ±10 kb 32.2% of significant deletions and 20.8% of significant insertions have a negative slope. Measurement presence tracks dosage in excess of the depth control at every interval width, so we report the chromosome-11, -17 and -19 loci as candidates.

Filter sensitivity comparison. For each trait, we computed the genomic-control factor λ GC = median(z 2 )/0.4549 over all (SV, trait) pairs for that trait, deflated each z to z/ √ λ GC , and applied Benjamini-Hochberg to the corrected P values at q < 0.05. A pair qualified as a candidate if it also passed the estimate_s_rss LD-consistency filter and CV R² ≥ 0.3 in both analyses. The ≥ 0.1 analysis therefore differs only in which predictors enter the joint fits and in each trait's test family: z is identical in all 2,957 SV-trait pairs common to the two analyses, and candidate status changes only because including additional predictors changes the calibration and multiple-testing correction.

Across the 191 traits tested in both, λ GC rose in 60 of the 70 traits that lost candidate SVtrait pairs (median ratio 1.15) and changed little in the 22 that gained (median 0.99; Spearman ρ = -0.69 between the λ GC ratio and the change in the number of candidates); because a per-trait rescaling is monotone, no trait both gained and lost. Supplementary Note 1: SV-caller comparison inside active α-satellite HOR arrays

To choose a caller for the catalog, we compared three assembly-based callers on the same HG002 HPRC Release 2 haplotype assemblies against CHM13 v2.0 [Nurk et al., 2022], with every callset restricted to the 62.25 Mb of active HOR array in CenSat v2.1 [Altemose et al., 2022]. SVIM-asm v1.0.3 [Heller and Vingron, 2021] ran per haplotype; PAV v2.4.6 [Ebert et al., 2021], applied genome-wide by HPRC Release 2 [Lucas et al., 2026], ran in a default and a tuned configuration; dipcall v0.3 [Li et al., 2018a] ran at default parameters, with no -x and no -z. PAV and dipcall each align the assemblies themselves, so assemblies, reference and HOR restriction are held constant; the alignments are not. SVIM-asm reports the most SVs at every cutoff through ≥ 100 kb (Table S1): 6,517 at ≥ 50 bp against 4,793 (PAV default) and 2,506 (dipcall), and 49 at ≥ 100 kb against 2 and 0. At ≥ 500 kb every caller reports zero non-breakend calls.

The tuned PAV run (-r 50000,500000, inv_region_limit 5 Mb, sized for HOR cores above 1.2 Mb) called fewer SVs than defaults at every cutoff from 1 to 50 kb (Table S1), and both configurations call the same two variants of at least 100 kb.

Within the arrays dipcall reports no SVs on chr1, chr5, chr6, chr13, chrX and chrY, although chr1, chr5, chr6 and chr13 contain 1,659, 1,420, 1,330 and 920 dipcall indels ≥ 50 bp genomewide. In high-identity arrays its alignment pileup either leaves the tandem repeats unaligned or GAP-filters the calls.

We applied the same SVIM-asm pipeline to the near-complete Q100 HG002 v1.1 maternal and paternal assemblies and compared the resulting calls with those from the HPRC Release 2 HG002 assemblies. In active HOR arrays the two callsets showed a positional agreement of 0.864 and Truvari [English et al., 2022] bench precision/recall/F1 of 0.842/0.824/0.833 (Table S2), a measure of reproducibility across assemblies of one individual. Against simulated SVs of known sequence, the same Truvari settings give precision/recall/F1 of 0.27/0.61/0.38 (Supplementary Note 13). HGSVC reported dipcall as the assembly-based caller with the highest false-positive rate [Logsdon et al., 2025].

We therefore used SVIM-asm for the catalog. The comparison is based on one individual, HG002, and the callers merge haplotypes differently, so differences in call counts should be interpreted qualitatively. SVIM-asm reclassifies events above its maximum SV size as breakends,

Supplementary Note 2: Assembly contiguity limits centromeric SV detection

Centromeric SV calling requires a contig that spans the HOR array; where an assembly terminates inside the array, SVIM-asm cannot emit a variant. We compared the HiFi HPRC Release 2 assemblies against the haplotype-resolved ONT R9.4.1 assemblies released by the 1000 Genomes ONT Sequencing Consortium [Gustafson et al., 2024], produced with Shasta [Shafin et al., 2020].

We measured the ONT assemblies to be 25-40× more fragmented than HiFi (ONT 2,503-3,300 contigs per haplotype, N50 ≈26-35 Mb; HiFi 74-120 contigs, N50 ≈134-149 Mb; Table S3). On chromosome 9 this reduced the median per-haplotype SV yield ∼6-fold (∼25 versus ∼150 calls), with tandem-array classes most depleted (DUP:TANDEM 13.9× fewer, breakends 12.4× fewer, versus 3.8× for all classes). This depletion is consistent with α-satellite array collapse. For a given locus and individual, when near-T2T HiFi assemblies of the same samples resolve the array as a single contig, we recover the haplogroups. HOR SV maps therefore require HiFi (or comparably contiguous) assemblies.

Supplementary Note 3: Locus mappability is the dominant determinant of imputation accuracy

We used two models to distinguish whether an SV is imputable from how accurately it is imputed.

The first model, classifying all 192,363 catalog SVs as imputable (5.6%) or not (Table S5), distinguished the two groups with a 5-fold ROC-AUC of 0.989 and relied primarily on sequencecomposition and chromosome features (GC content, active HOR span, satellite complexity), not allele frequency. In the second model, adding contig-level alignment features (mean MAPQ, fraction of secondary alignments, contig count, and edit distance at the locus) raised the held-out R² of the imputation-accuracy model from 0.407 to 0.457. The fraction of secondary alignments became the single most important predictor (permutation-importance 0.133; Supplementary Fig. S3, Table S6), while the top sequence-composition feature (GC content over 10 kb) fell from first to fifth in importance. In grouped drop-column tests the mapping-quality family contributed the largest single-group loss (∆R² = -0.054, 2.2× that of GC), and the three feature families together explained roughly half the modeled variance. GC content is therefore largely a proxy for mapping ambiguity in repetitive sequence. In the Q100 HG002 assembly, we reproduced imputable SVs at a higher rate than unimputable ones (0.904 versus 0.848, +0.055), but a chromosome-block bootstrap CI included zero ([-0.011, +0.124]).

Supplementary Note 4: Comparison with a reference-panel copying model (Beagle)

To compare imputation accuracy, we benchmarked the per-SV elastic net against Beagle 5 [Browning et al., 2018], a Li-Stephens copying model [Li and Stephens, 2003], on the identical SVs, pericentromeric SNPs and shared SNP set. Reconstructing SNP-SV phase from the assembly-to-reference alignments raised the SV-SNP r 2 from 0.58 to 0.86 (SNP-SNP control 0.99), and held-out common SNPs imputed at r 2 0.93-0.97 as a positive control. We ran S7). The elastic net was more robust than Beagle when each superpopulation was held out in turn. Beagle requires the assembly-co-phased panel, built from the same assemblies it imputes, while the elastic net uses SNP genotypes alone.

To test whether the QTL signal depends on how variants are defined, we repeated the QTL mapping with a genotyping route that reads centromere haplogroups directly from short-read k-mers (ascairn [Shiraishi et al., 2026]).
