Supplementary Note 6: Distal cis associations and controls

We asked whether distal cis and trans associations survive controls for tag SNPs and paralogs.

Two distance metrics in cis. Every centromeric SV is anchored at its chromosome's centromere midpoint for cis-region construction, so the distance the QTL mapping reports is distance to the centromere. Because an imputed dosage is a linear function of its tag SNPs, we also computed distance to the nearest tag SNP of its elastic-net model, restricted to the 3,905 of 3,949 model SNPs (98.9%) present in the 1000 Genomes phased panel; SNPs absent from the panel are represented as constant columns and cannot contribute. Of all 166 significant cis gene associations across the two imputation ensembles, 35 lie ≥ 10 Mb from the centromere, and 14 lie ≥ 10 Mb from the centromere and from every tag SNP, at 11 independent loci, with distances ranging 12.2-132.4 Mb.

We refit every significant cis pair conditioning on the model's tag SNPs (Supplementary Fig. S7). The refit reproduces the main analysis (Pearson r = 0.997 between refit and original -log 10 P ; significance recovered in 430 of 430 pairs). Conditioning on all of the model's local tag SNPs is degenerate by construction, so we classified each fit by the R² of the dosage on its conditioners (informative < 0.90, marginal 0.90-0.99, degenerate ≥ 0.99), and excluded degenerate fits. Conditioning on all local tag SNPs leaves 42 of 124 testable eQTL pairs (33.9%) and 45 of 100 sQTL pairs (45.0%) significant; conditioning on the single nearest tag SNP leaves Supplementary Note 7: Supporting analyses for the chromosome-8 centromere-dip-position locus

The Li-Ji effective number of independent phenotypes is 6.0, and the significant lead variants reach the 10 -7 permutation floor and the significant set is unchanged when correction uses seven, eight or ten phenotypes. We asked whether this association is robust, whether the deletion can be distinguished from linked SNPs, and what sequence underlies it.

Robustness of the chromosome-8 association

A chromosome-8 locus is associated with CDR position. The lead deletion lies in a 213.6 kb interval at chr8:44.25-44.46 Mb.

It contains every study-wide-significant chromosome-8 lead from all eight CDR phenotypes.

Within it, five distinct genotype vectors on four SVs produce nine significant (genotype-group × phenotype) associations (Extended Data Table 1; Figure 4a, b): four vectors under both position phenotypes, and a 1,868-bp insertion under the deepest-dip phenotype alone; the insertion at chr8:44,302,147 reaches the threshold under two independently derived genotype vectors. Outside this interval, leads on chromosomes 5, 9 and 19 also reach study-wide significance under the canonical covered-length frame; each loses it in the robustness analysis (Extended Data Fig. 1).

The chromosome-8 association is concordant across five superpopulations. It is permutation-calibrated at 10 7 draws over the complete catalog, stable when the array endpoints are modeled, homogeneous across five superpopulations (concordant in all five, t from -2.06 to -4.58; inverse-variance meta-analysis z = -6.56, P = 5.3 × 10 -11 ; Cochran Q P = 0.50) and specific to dip position among eight phenotypes. The association identifies the locus but does not distinguish among its linked variants. At r = 0.95 the 113-bp deletion and its linked chromosome-8 pericentromeric variants share the same signal in this cohort, and dip position is measured relative to the annotated array.

The locus has a single signal. The 113-bp deletion and its tag SNP show similar associations with CDR position (P ≈ 10 -7 for each). In African-ancestry samples linkage partially breaks down (r² = 0.67) and the SNP survives joint fitting while the deletion loses significance (P = 0.033, n = 41); in East Asian and European samples the pair is collinear. The interval contains a single independent signal. Conditioning each pre-specified lead on the top lead leaves three with a nominal conditional association (P = 0.019-0.041), the strongest the 347-bp deletion at chr8:44,460,941 (|r| = 0.62). Calibrated against the set screened, the best of these is P = 0.10 over the pre-specified leads and P = 0.61 over all 69 genotype vectors in the interval.

Specificity to dip position

The chromosome-8 association is specific to dip position. Of the four aspects of CDR organization measured (Extended Data Table 2), only position shows a significant association.

The chromosome-8 leads show no association with dip spread, dip count, dip width, the hypomethylated fraction or bulk methylation (lead deletion P = 0.59 for hypomethylated fraction, 0.15 for mean 5mC, 0.52 for dip width, 0.24-0.96 for dip count; Extended Data Fig. 1).

Dip position is dosage-dependent at the chromosome-8 leads: the median relative dip position is 0.82, 0.71 and 0.55 across the three dosage classes of the lead deletion (Figure 4c).

Chromosome-8 array length is independent of dosage. The chromosome-8 locus alone has this property (|t| ≤ 1.00, P ≥ 0.32). Total SV burden predicts array length (t = +11.95), no burden association remains significant once length is in the model (Figure 4e), and length variation is uncorrelated with assembly coverage (r = -0.03, n = 181).

For mean 5mC across the array (Supplementary Fig. S17), the SV association analysis shows little genomic inflation (λ = 0.948, median P = 0.49), and aggregate burden, associated with mean 5mC at P = 1.8 × 10 -9 , reaches P ≈ 0.08 after array-length adjustment, with a smaller individual-level component at P = 0.003. Contig count predicts mean 5mC and array length (t = +4.5, +6.3) and explains R² = 0.02 of burden.

In analyses partitioned by individual and chromosome, dip position has an intraclass correlation of 0.000 and mean 5mC of 0.91, and adjusting either for array length leaves both unchanged; dip position can differ between homologs within an individual, consistent with a cis-acting effect.

Partitioning variation in the same way distinguishes two contributions of array length: it accounts for 54% of the between-superpopulation difference in the hypomethylated fraction and 42% in dip density, the two phenotypes that divide by it, and none of the difference in mean 5mC, which remains an individual-level trait that differs among superpopulations after adjustment (R² = 0.083, P = 0.004).

No chromosome-8 SV reaches the threshold at any of the three interval widths of the localmethylation test (Supplementary Note 11), on a set that tests all 272 of its SVs at n = 130. The mediation analysis provides no evidence that local methylation level explains the chromosome-8 association with dip position. Across all four leads the direct effect equals the total, the SV-to-methylation step has P = 0.39-0.89, and the indirect effect's confidence interval spans zero.

Three further loci associate on arrays whose length or boundaries vary with dosage.

Leads on chromosomes 5, 9 and 19 rank highest outside the chromosome-8 interval, though the chromosome-19 lead loses significance once the array endpoints are added as covariates. Their arrays change length with dosage, and normalizing by array length cannot distinguish a shift in dip position from a change in total array length. The chromosome-5 lead is the only one whose association weakens after adjustment (t = +5.32 → +4.09, P = 1 × 10 -6 → 4.2 × 10 -5 ), and the basis of this association remains unclear.

Cis effects on the haplotype with the deletion Dip position differs between homologs by deletion status. In the 15 individuals heterozygous for the lead deletion, the two homologs of a single nucleus have relative dip positions of 0.516 and 0.819 (paired difference -0.309, Wilcoxon P = 3.0 × 10 -4 ; the homolog with the deletion closer to the center of the array in 13 of the 15). Using the two centromere groups in place of the deletion gives 27 heterozygotes and the same result (difference -0.253, Wilcoxon P = 4.9 × 10 -7 , 24 of 27), equal in size to the difference between unrelated individuals.

Dip position differs by SV-defined centromere group. Grouping haplotypes by neighbor-joining on cosine distances over the chromosome-8 SV matrix gives two SV-defined centromere groups, with the 113-bp deletion present on every haplotype in one group. Nineteen haplotypes in the other group also have the deletion, allowing a within-group comparison. Using assembly sequence between unique flanking 31-mers, we genotyped the deletion and found a mean relative dip position among carriers of 0.834, indistinguishable from the 64 non-carriers of the same group (0.837). The deletion's effect within a group is estimated at -1% of the between-group difference (bootstrap 95% CI -22% to +10%), and dip position is associated with the SV-defined group. Because every haplotype in the first group has the deletion, only sufficiency on the alternative background is testable, not necessity. A further 12 carriers in the same group had no dip called, at a rate indistinguishable from non-carriers (61% against 73%, Fisher P = 0.26).

Modification-call filtering and ONT chemistry.

With methylation computed from 5mC calls alone (Methods), dip counts agree between the R9.4.1 and R10.4.1 cohorts (rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.99-1.10; array methylation P = 0.15 adjusting for ancestry).

Trans association analysis. We tested each locus against every off-chromosome phenotype, 2,045,280 trans tests in 192 chromosome-phenotype pairs. Because a Bonferroni threshold at that test count (2.4 × 10 -8 ) is below the minimum P value attainable with the available permutations, the main statistic is the global maximum |t| over 100,000 permutations shared across the whole panel. The analysis is calibrated (median λ = 1.013; 19,852 sub-threshold candidates at P ≤ 0.01 against 20,453 expected), its cis positive control places the chromosome-8 leads at the top of 88,952 tests, and every trans test has family-wise error ≥ 0.05 and q ≥ 0.05, the strongest being an insertion at chr20:28,704,151 against chromosome-21 dip width (P = 4.1×10 -7 , familywise error 0.14).

Supplementary Note 8: Supporting analyses for the biobank-scale disease screen

The score test gave conservative or well-calibrated results relative to the exact Firth fit within each carrier-count bin and predictor set.

One hundred seventy associations, most of them protective. At q < 0.05, 170 SVphecode associations are significant, spanning 61 distinct SVs and 27 phecodes, with a further 85 associations at0.05 ≤ q < 0.10 (Figure 6a).

Of the 170 associations, 110 were protective. The 61 significant SVs have a median crossvalidated imputation R² of 0.23, with 38 below 0.30 and 11 at 0.45 or better (accounting for 45 associations).

Chromosomes 11 and 19 contribute 1,022 and 1,058 SV-phecode pairs at P ≤ 10 -4 , of which two and none, respectively, are significant, compared with 134 of 407 for chromosome 16.

A set of 3,097 pericentromeric SVs with no summary-level signal shows no association at q < 0.05 and none at q < 0.10 across 7,485,449 tests (Figure 6b). Its smallest P is 4.5 × 10 -8 against 1.3 × 10 -7 expected for the minimum of that many tests under the null, a value reached by chance with probability 0.29. These predictors are imputed as well as the discovery predictors, at a median cross-validated R² of 0.30 against 0.21. The procedure is therefore calibrated on panel collinearity positively correlated (r = +0.179).

Of 46 localization instances, 15 arise under both panel constructions, 21 occur under the single-SV panel alone and 10 under the joint panel alone. Seven of the 10 are candidates on chromosomes 16 and X with marginal support from P = 1.2 × 10 -6 to 6.2 × 10 -13 that have higher posterior support than other SVs in the model; of the three outside the candidate set, a chromosome-16 SV with alcohol abuse and dependence reaches joint posterior 1.00 at marginal P = 0.94 within a cluster of collinear SVs, and two show marginal signal (P = 2.2 × 10 -8 and 2.4 × 10 -6 ) at negligible posterior.

Supplementary Note 9: Measurement availability at candidate CpGs depends on carrier status

Because the methylation-QTL analysis estimates each CpG effect among individuals with a measurement, we tested whether measurement depended on genotype at the associated SV. Supplementary Fig. S11 measures this dependence in 150 HPRC Release 2 individuals with assembly-derived genotypes, all distinct from the 124 discovery individuals. The per-pair slope of measurement presence on carrier dosage is negative in 302 of the 354 testable discovery pairs (85.3%), against a matched null of twenty control CpGs per discovery CpG (6,280 pairs over 4,715 control CpGs) whose rate falls below nominal under one shared Benjamini-Hochberg family. Measurement availability is associated with the sign of the discovery effect (Fisher odds ratio 15.55, P = 8.9 × 10 -26 ). The target CpGs lie outside the deleted interval of their source SV in 465 of 465 pairs, so missing methylation calls cannot be explained by deletion of the target CpG. The assayed pericentromeric region spans 6.8 Mb per contig, and this window excludes the more distal pairs at which the discovery effect was hypermethylating.

A within-individual test comparing the between-haplotype methylation difference of SV heterozygotes with that of homozygotes detected an association at ∼40% of the SVs shared between the methylation and expression analyses, a pattern that R9.4.1 5mC miscalling would also produce.

We estimated per-CpG effects in the discovery cohort alone because estimates from the HPRC cohort would include bias from differential measurement availability.

For each matched trait, high posterior inclusion probabilities (PIP) for individual SVs were cohort-specific.

After re-fitting against a panel of ∼12,000 SNPs from the same region (Methods), most joint candidate associations returned a credible set that spanned collinear variants. Of 473 single-SV candidate hits and 3,688 joint candidate hits, 36 (10 SVs) and 17 (3 SVs), respectively, retained PIP > 0.5. Among the remaining 3,671 joint SV-trait pairs (all 3,688 pairs but the 17 that retained PIP > 0.5), 63.6% returned unresolved credible sets in which the collinear pericentromeric LD left multiple credible variants (SV or SNP). A further 22.2% failed to converge, and in 14.2% a specific SNP received higher posterior support than the SV (Supplementary Fig. S5).

The SV lay inside a credible set in 90.4% of unresolved SV-trait pairs against 67.7% of pairs in which a SNP received higher posterior support (robust to a sensitivity re-fit and a lower inclusion threshold; Supplementary Note 11). Most joint candidate associations therefore implicate a set of linked pericentromeric variants without distinguishing the SV from nearby SNPs.

Two SVs passed all three analyses, one on a single trait and one on multiple traits. The first, a chromosome-11 deletion (CV R² = 0.41), passed on one trait. The second, an insertion in the chromosome-19 pericentromere, passed on 26, 15 and 12 traits in the three analyses at CV R² = 0.999, with a median dense-panel PIP of 0.999 (range 0.79-1.00; ≥ 0.98 in 21 of its 26 single-SV traits). The SNPs used to impute it span a 4.5-Mb haplotype (GRCh38 chr19:23.9-28.4 Mb) straddling the centromere and tags at least two independent association peaks ∼3 Mb apart, and at CV R² ≈ 1 the SV itself lies within the span of those predictor SNPs. The insertion therefore marks a recombination-suppressed block across the centromere. The trait association is localized to the haplotype block marked by the insertion. Distinguishing the insertion from other variants in this block requires direct genotyping across the region.

S10.2 Overview and design

We tested whether pericentromeric structural variants (SVs) are associated with human complex traits by integrating SV dosages, imputed from local single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), with publicly available GWAS summary statistics in a causal TWAS (cTWAS) framework [Zhao et al., 2024]. SV dosages are not present in GWAS cohorts; we therefore (i) trained per-SV elastic-net predictors from flanking SNPs, (ii) formed an augmented summary-statistic and LD representation in which each SV occupies one row/column alongside the SNPs, and (iii) jointly fine-mapped SNPs and SVs per genomic region with the "regression with summary statistics" model SuSiE-RSS [Wang et al., 2020 , Zou et al., 2022].

Two properties of these data determine the analysis design. First, the imputed-SV summary statistic is a deterministic linear combination of the same SNP statistics that are included in the LD matrix, so the augmented LD matrix is rank-deficient and the SV signal is collinear with its tagging SNPs (Sections S10.6-S10.7). Second, GWAS support is frequently missing across these low-complexity intervals, and how missing summary statistics are handled materially changes the result (Section S10.9). We therefore treat calibration (Section S10.10), power and limits on distinguishing SVs from their tag SNPs (Section S10.11), and an assessment of whether associations can be attributed specifically to SVs (Section S10.13) as part of the method.

S10.3 Datasets and accessions

All input datasets are public; accessions and versions are given in Table S15.

S10.6 The augmented cTWAS / SuSiE-RSS model

Within a super-region of p SNPs and G jointly fine-mapped SVs, the SNP GWAS z-scores z ∈ R p , the SNP LD matrix R ∈ R p×p , and the G predictor weight vectors β 1 , . . . , β G are combined into an augmented z-vector z aug ∈ R p+G and an augmented correlation matrix R aug ∈ R (p+G) ×(p+G) that treat each SV as a single "synthetic variant." This follows the FUSION/S-PrediXcan imputed-association identity [Gusev et al., 2016 , Barbeira et al., 2018] and the multi-feature canonical construction of cTWAS [Zhao et al., 2024], generalized to G ≥ 1 correlated SVs (Supplementary Fig. S19a).

Summary-statistic imputation is a single-variant estimator, and feeding imputed z into the joint SuSiE-RSS likelihood risks miscalibration if the imputation uncertainty is not modeled [Kartau and Pirinen, 2025]; the calibration experiments quantify this (Section S10.10).

S10.10 Calibration: null designs and false-positive rates

We characterized the false-positive (FP) behavior of each handling with three nested null designs, each drawing 230 replicate z-vectors and recording FP@τ = Pr(PIP SV ≥ τ | no SV is causal) at τ = 0.8 (Table S19).

1. Global null (pure noise, no signal): z ∼ N (0, R). Tests whether a handling produces false positives from noise. 2. Regional-signal null (one observed causal SNP c, all SVs null):

Tests whether real regional signal is mis-attributed to an SV.

3. Missing-causal-lead null. The causal lead is absent from the GWAS (≥ 84% of predictor support missing). PAD assigns it a zero z-score, IMPUTE estimates it, and MATCHED excludes it.

Supplementary Note 11: Sensitivity analyses

Merged CDR calls reproduce the chromosome-8 association. Gao et al. [2026] merge hypomethylated calls within 150 kb into a single CDR; ours are the unmerged dips. Applying their merge reduces 22,537 dips across 5,034 active arrays to 5,400 CDRs, a mean of 1.07 per array, and widens the median call from 30 kb to 215 kb.

We recomputed every phenotype from the merged calls and repeated the association analysis with the same genotypes, covariates, permutation seed and null. The chromosome-8 lead is unchanged (t = -6.173 against t = -6.172) and the study-wide significant set for dip position is identical on chromosomes 8 and 5, with no locus gained (Supplementary Fig. S15); of the four chromosome-8 loci in Extended Data Table 1 the 1,868 bp insertion alone loses significance.

After merging, the two position phenotypes are identical on 93.3% of arrays, against 17.4% before.

Local methylation intervals. Testing methylation in intervals around each SV assesses local associations separately from the array-wide mean (Supplementary Note 7). In 192 individuals with assembly-derived SV genotypes, we tested each SV against mean 5mC in ±10, ±50 and ±100 kb intervals around it. The tests used Minigraph-Cactus chains or the SVIM-asm alignments used for SV calling, with at least 50 individuals per test. We applied Bonferroni correction within each interval width and, in a sensitivity analysis, across all three widths; we assessed significance using 10 7 permutations. We required each candidate to show no significant association with sequencing depth, and used a second control to test whether SV dosage predicted the availability of a methylation value. In intervals around each SV, three loci reach the threshold at 10 7 permutations in the SVIM-asm alignments, which make 9,889-10,499 loci testable; the Minigraph-Cactus chain spans α-satellite on a subset of chromosomes, reaches n ≥ 50 at 12.4% of the catalog with chromosomes 1, 4 and 17 untested, and gives a null result at every scale. The three loci are an insertion at chr11:54,314,992 (P = 1-2×10 -6 ), an insertion at chr17:26,767,558 and a deletion at chr19:28,468,779, and all three are associated with lower methylation at higher SV dosage. The chromosome-11 and chromosome-19 associations remain significant after correction across the three interval widths. The coverage negative control showed a larger excess of associations than methylation at every interval width.

Supplementary Note 12: Population differentiation of centromeric SVs

S12.1 Highly differentiated QTL SVs cluster at a few loci, most prominently on chromosome 10

Structural variants can track population structure [Almarri et al., 2020], which makes allelefrequency differentiation a relevant property of each SV associated with expression or splicing.

Each SV is described by its maximum pairwise F ST across the five 1000 Genomes superpopulations (Section S12.2).

Centromeric SVs show low population differentiation. Across the full catalog the mean F ST was 0.0164, 0.58% had F ST > 0.15, and the most differentiated variant reached F ST = 0.580 (Supplementary Fig. S21). On average, imputable SVs were more differentiated (mean 0.0238; 1.47% above 0.15), and that excess was spread across centromeres and imputation-accuracy levels (Supplementary Fig. S21). At the stringent imputability threshold (CV R² ≥ 0.3), SVs associated with expression or splicing were enriched 2.9-fold for high-F ST variants relative to SVs passing the same threshold (6 of 106 above F ST = 0.15, 5.66% against a 1.99% background; one-sided Fisher P = 1.7 × 10 -2 ); at the permissive threshold (CV R² ≥ 0.1) the corresponding ratio was 1.4 (4 of 182, 2.20% against 1.62%; P = 0.34).

S12.2 Population differentiation analysis

To assess whether centromeric-SV associations reflect population structure, we computed the single-locus F ST for each SV using the Hudson estimator [Bhatia et al., 2013], from directly called HPRC SVIM-asm genotypes rather than imputed dosages. We computed SV allele frequencies in the 188 HPRC training individuals, partitioned into five 1000 Genomes superpopulations (AFR = 55, AMR = 39, EAS = 39, SAS = 34, EUR = 21). For a pair of superpopulations (i, j) with alternate-allele frequencies p i , p j over n i , n j diploid individuals, the Hudson estimator is with each frequency estimated as p = g g / (2n) over diploid genotypes g ∈ {0, 1, 2}, so that the sampling-variance correction applies to the 2n sampled gene copies.

We summarized each SV by its maximum F ST across the ten superpopulation pairs and classified SVs with F ST > 0.15 as highly differentiated. We retained negative per-pair estimates, which arise as sampling noise when differentiation is near zero, without truncation. We tested enrichment of QTL hits for differentiated SVs with a one-sided Fisher exact test on the 2 × 2 table of (hit vs. non-hit) × (high-vs. low-F ST ) over the imputable SV analysis set, separately for the permissive (CV R² ≥ 0.1) and strict (CV R² ≥ 0.3) imputability levels. We matched QTL hits to the frequency table using the identifier the QTL analysis itself assigns each tested unit (chromosome and within-chromosome SV index), which is one-to-one.

Supplementary Note 13: Accuracy of SVIM-asm calls inside active HOR arrays

Simulation design. We simulated CHM13 chromosomes 1-22 and X with clustered substitutions at 0, 1 and 2% in the active HOR array and 0.1% elsewhere. We introduced 12-15 SVs of known sequence per simulated chromosome (1,017 in total), comprising insertions, deletions, tandem and dispersed duplications, inversions and complex replacements of 50 bp to 100 kb with α-satellite inserted sequence (Supplementary Table S22). A matched negative control for each chromosome contained no simulated SVs. We aligned all chromosomes to CHM13 and processed them with the catalog pipeline (Methods).

Scoring. Because the same sequence change can have several equivalent representations within a tandem repeat, we scored the reconstructed sequence rather than requiring identical breakpoint coordinates. We considered a simulated SV detected when the reported calls, applied to the reference, reconstructed its sequence exactly; we accepted shifted breakpoints along the repeat and split representations. With P the simulated SVs, E the reported calls and U the negativecontrol units (whole arrays and 50-kb windows), where P rec are detected SVs, E match calls contributing to a reconstruction and U 0 units without calls.

We scored calls with an unresolved match (101 of 2,055) as incorrect. Recall measures the fraction of introduced changes reconstructed exactly, whereas precision measures the fraction of reported calls contributing to those reconstructions. Thus, a large event reported as several incorrect small calls can reduce both recall and precision.

Accuracy in simulation.

Recall decreased with SV size and background divergence, and the pipeline detected no inversions or complex replacements (Supplementary Fig. S22b; Supplementary Table S22). Precision varied widely among chromosomes (Supplementary Fig. S22a), and the caller frequently represented large simulated SVs as multiple small incorrect calls. Truvari with the settings of the HG002 comparison yielded a similar precision (Table S2). Negative controls were free of calls in 59 of 69 arrays. The low precision despite few calls in negative controls suggests that alignment and representation of true structural changes within repeats contribute to errors. Agreement between assemblies of the same individual (Supplementary Note 1) therefore measures reproducibility, which can exceed accuracy against known sequence changes.

Frequency filtering. In a simulated cohort of 256 haplotypes merged and filtered as for the catalog, carrier-level precision increased from 30% to 53% at a minimum minor allele frequency of 5%, whereas recall of rare SVs decreased (Supplementary Fig. S22c). Haplotypes of the same lineage frequently shared incorrect common calls. Frequency filtering therefore enriches for accurate calls but also retains systematic errors shared within lineages. Such calls may predict haplotype membership without correctly specifying the underlying structural change; imputation accuracy alone cannot establish sequence-level accuracy.

Sequence composition and length periodicity. We annotated the changed sequence of each call (inserted sequence for insertions, removed CHM13 sequence for deletions) with Re-peatMasker 4.1.9; we classified calls with ≥80% of these bases annotated as α-satellite or transposable element accordingly. We considered a length L periodic at period P and tolerance t when min k≥1 |L -kP | ≤ t; control periods and the expectation under uniformly distributed lengths, (2t + 1)/P , provide null comparisons (Supplementary Table S23; Supplementary Fig. S22d).

Enrichment near multiples of 171 bp is consistent with gains and losses of α-satellite monomers.

Storey and Tibshirani, 2003] (q < 0.05). In trans, we tested each centromeric SV against genes and splicing phenotypes on all other chromosomes. We retained pairs at nominal P < 10 -5 and declared trans genes significant at a genome-wide threshold of P < 5 × 10 -8 . We included SVs with CV R² ≥ 0.1 and carrier frequency in [0.05, 0.99]. We further assessed trans associations using Benjamini-Hochberg and Bonferroni correction over the full number of SV-phenotype pairs tested, cross-mappability between each target gene and the pericentromere of the SV's own chromosome[Saha and Battle, 2018a], conditioning on the tag SNPs of the SV's imputation model, and a search of the complete CHM13 assembly (minimap2 -x asm20 -N 50) for paralogs of the target locus that GRCh38 omits; the same paralog search was applied to distal cis genes against the pericentromere of their own chromosome. We assessed calibration using genomiccontrol λ for the per-gene Beta-approximated permutation P values (Supplementary Note 6).

inverse-normal transformed burden per (individual, chromosome) and each phenotype within chromosome and fit y ic ∼ burden cis,ic +burden trans,i(-c) +quality+10 GRM PCs+(1 | individual) over 3,123 individual-by-chromosome rows, separating centromere-local from systemic or technical effects, with assembly-quality terms included. We confirmed significance using 1,000 individual-label shuffles and re-fitted every burden association with array length as a covariate; we report the adjusted estimates.Conditional analysis and fine-mapping of the chromosome-8 locus.To ask whether the chromosome-8 lead is attributable to the deletion or to SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with it, we applied the same three-part evaluation used for the methylation-QTL leads (see Methylation-QTL association testing), against the identical association model (rank-inversenormal dip position, intercept, ten ancestry principal components and a basecaller indicator). We used assembly-derived deletion genotypes. Each of the ten pericentromeric SNP panels used for conditioning (namely fixed intervals of 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1 and 2 Mb, the nearest 500, 1,000 and 2,000 SNPs to each centromere boundary, and the nearest 500 and 1,000 to the midpoint) served in turn as the competitor set. Within each panel we (i) fitted SuSiE jointly over the SV and up to 300 selected SNPs and read the SV posterior inclusion probability and credible-set assignment, (ii) conditioned on up to 20 SNPs pruned greedily from the strongest at |r| < 0.8, and (iii) ran a five-fold cross-fitted ridge residual test with a heteroskedasticity-robust score standard error. In (iii), covariate coefficients and SNP selection are estimated within each training fold and applied to held-out samples. We also report the maximum absolute correlation between the deletion and any single panel SNP, together with the number of individuals with discordant genotypes at the two.

Figure 1 :

Figure 1: Centromeric structural-variant discovery, imputation and association with gene expression and disease. a Variant calling. Haplotype-resolved HPRC long-read assemblies were aligned to the telomere-to-telomere CHM13 reference, and structural variants were called within the active αsatellite higher-order-repeat (HOR) core with SVIM-asm, resulting in 188,589 centromeric SVs across chromosomes 1-22 and X. b The 1,967 monophyletic components resolved from complex multi-allelic SVs by per-chromosome neighbor-joining of centromeric haplotypes. c Pericentromeric predictor SNP sets, defined by three strategies (fixed flanking interval; boundary-anchored count; midpoint-anchored count). SNPs were extracted from the pericentromeric interval flanking each SV under each strategy, and the model with the highest cross-validated R² among eight candidates was retained for that SV. d Per-SV elastic-net imputation into 630 unrelated 1000 Genomes samples. Models were fitted on the 188 HPRC individuals with matched SNPs under 4-fold cross-validation, and imputed SV dosage was used for the samples with matched MAGE expression and splicing. e Imputed SVs were tested as cisand trans-QTLs for gene expression (eQTL) and RNA splicing (sQTL). f Imputed SV dosage was tested for disease association in All of Us participants and fine-mapped against the highly-correlated and tagged SNPs of each SV under in-sample LD.

Figure 2: Centromeric structural variants in the active satellite array are linked to pericentromeric SNPs, and phylogenetic resolution improves SV imputation. a Each bar shows one chromosome at true length on a shared CHM13 v2.0 axis, filled by its SV-type composition and labeled with its total SV count. Notches mark the centromere, drawn wider than the arrays themselves (0.34-4.97 Mb on chromosomes of 45-248 Mb) so that they remain visible. b, c Pairwise LD (Pearson r) among pericentromeric SNPs and centromeric SVs across the chromosome-19 (b) and chromosome-11 (c) centromeres in the 188 individuals with assembled SVs and 1000 Genomes genotypes. Blocks were thinned; the SVs shown are the highest-frequency variants and the SNPs those most correlated. d Schematic of a resolvable SV, carriers forming a monophyletic clade (green), separated by resolution as an imputable component, off-clade carriers as a residual. An unresolved SV has carriers scattered across clades. e Mean cross-validated R² by class (eight-model ensemble, 4-fold CV). Monophyletic components (n = 1,967) reach 0.407 compared with 0.371 for the same SVs before resolution (n = 2,032); unresolved SVs (n = 16,609) 0.065; residual components (n = 359) 0.078. f Advantage of monophyletic components over their own higher-frequency pre-resolution parents and over unresolved SVs in every carrier-frequency bin. The most differentiated hits cluster at a few loci. A chromosome-10 insertion at ∼39.6 Mb (F ST = 0.580, depleted on African haplotypes) tags the ZNF33A association, an adjacent 1,357bp insertion 163 bp away (F ST = 0.292) tags TMEM273 /HSD17B7P2 /GTF2IP, and further differentiated SVs lie on chromosomes 1 and 6 (F ST ≈ 0.20). The SVs associated with SUV39H1 (F ST = 0.00) and the chromosome-20 TTPAL/PLTP /NEURL2 splicing trio (F ST ≤ 0.04) fall in the undifferentiated majority. Population differentiation among QTL SVs is concentrated in a small set of loci, most prominently on chromosome 10.
